title: 2025-06-03 POC Weekly Sync - Caching & Prompt Reuse
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on caching telemetry and prompt reuse. Redwood and Payload reviewed KV/prefix cache hit rates, identified templating issues causing low reuse, validated a change to prompt canonicalization, and agreed to run a 24h live benchmark with new hashing and canonical prompts. Security and integration notes: customer wants KMS key rotation details and confirmation on audit logs for private deployment. Next steps: run 24h benchmark, share updated benchmark sheet, schedule performance deep dive with infra team, send security docs.

Redwood: share updated benchmarks spreadsheet and raw telemetry link (Maya)

action_items: Liam O'Connor - implement prompt canonicalization + new KV hash and start 24h run - due 2025-06-05

transcript:
[00:00] Maya: ok everyone, thanks for joining. this is the weekly poc caching sync for Payload. we’ll run about 45 minutes. Liam and I from Redwood, and then Sarah, Tom, Priya from Payload. quick sound check?
[00:12] Sarah: sounds good, can hear you.
[00:14] Tom: yep good here.
[00:16] Liam: great, i’ll kick off with the telemetry summary. we pulled last 7 days of KV and prefix cache metrics. overall kv hit rate is about 18% across the board, prefix cache around 12%.
[00:30] Sarah: uh that seems low vs our expectations. we were expecting like 40-50% reuse because many prompts are templated.
[00:38] Liam: same. we dug into it and found two things: one, prompt variability due to user-generated fields (timestamps, ids) that break the prefix match; two, client-side templating sometimes inlines slightly different spacing/punctuation which prevents canonical matching.
[00:55] Maya: to be clear, when we say prefix cache here we’re referring to the first N tokens we keep in the KV store for reuse between requests with common prefixes, yes?
[01:02] Liam: yes, exactly. prefix caching is our short-term prefix match that avoids recomputation of early context. kv cache covers longer-range key/value KV entries for multi-turn sessions.
[01:10] Diego (customer, interject): i’m seeing lots of low frequency prompts because some product events append a UUID. that explains a lot.
[01:18] Sarah: yep. we have a mix of funnel events and free-text notes. we can probably standardize the funnel ones.
[01:23] Liam: ok good. second thing: we noticed the client does not send a stable template identifier in headers, so our cache key is the raw prompt text. when the client adds small variation the key differs and you lose the hit.
[01:36] Maya: so the remediation is twofold: canonicalize prompts before sending, and/or have client send a template_id header so the runtime can map to the same cache key.
[01:45] Priya: would that work for hosted calls and dedicated? we’re running the POC on Redwood hosted now but may move to dedicated later.
[01:52] Liam: yes both. template_id is just metadata. in dedicated we can also configure more aggressive prefix lengths and different eviction policy.
[01:59] Tom: curious about batching — if we batch requests more aggressively does that change hit rates? we’re trying to balance latency and unit cost.
[02:07] Liam: batching can help throughput but it doesn't increase prefix hit rate unless the batched requests share identical prefixes. batching is orthogonal; however, batching increases the chance of reuse of KV cache across parallel requests if sessions are similar. but in your case, canonicalization gains are larger.
[02:23] Sarah: can you show a quick before/after example of canonicalization?
[02:26] Liam: sure. example: original prompt: "Summarize customer event 2025-05-30T13:22:11Z id=abc-123: user reported..." canonicalized: "Summarize customer event <TIMESTAMP> id=<UUID>: user reported...". we replace high-entropy tokens with placeholders and then hash the template. that yields the same cache key across minor variations.
[02:48] Sarah: makes sense. is there a risk of over-canonicalizing and losing specificity we need in the model?
[02:53] Liam: good question. we only canonicalize stable template parts — we leave slots for variables that are injected into the model inputs as separate tokens so the model still sees the unique data. canonicalization only affects how we compute the cache key and prefix hash, not the actual input fed to the model.
[03:07] Tom: ok, the telemetry you mentioned — do you have concrete numbers if we apply canonicalization?
[03:12] Liam: in a lab run with 100k requests, when we canonicalized and used template_id headers, kv hit rate jumped from 17% to 53% and prefix hit from 11% to 39% for that workload. caveat: this was an offline lab with representative but not complete production distribution.
[03:30] Sarah: that’s promising. did you tune eviction policies as part of that?
[03:34] Liam: yes we adjusted lru window and increased prefix retention window from 60s to 180s for the test, which helped for short-lived conversational flows. but the biggest delta came from canonicalization.
[03:45] Maya: noted. are there any side effects on latency variability?
[03:49] Liam: minimal. canonicalization is a tiny CPU op on the client or on the edge, sub-ms at scale. increased prefix retention slightly increases memory usage on the server side but within your Dedicated plan quotas it was fine. on hosted it's configurable per-customer.
[04:03] Priya: about config — for dedicated we want to know about cache eviction metrics and how to tune them. can Redwood expose those metrics to our console?
[04:11] Maya: yes, through the Console we can surface per-customer cache hit rate, eviction counts, memory utilization and tail latency. we'll provide a dashboard link in the benchmarks sheet.
[04:20] Tom: security items — we want to ensure key material and audit logs. specifically KMS rotation policy and audit trails for who accessed the cache or changed policies.
[04:29] Liam: we log cache configuration changes in admin audit logs and support KMS integrations. for Private we can integrate with your HSM/KMS and enable rotation. for hosted we offer managed KMS or customer-managed keys through our KMS integration.
[04:40] Sarah: can you send a short doc about KMS rotation and what audit entries look like?
[04:43] Maya: yes, I’ll include that in the follow-up.
[04:45] Diego: one more telemetry note — some requests are failing to get KV entries because the prompt length surpasses our prefix window. can we increase the prefix window per-model?
[04:53] Liam: yes, prefix window and token windows are configurable per model instance. increasing it helps reuse for long prompts but increases memory. we can recommend a value based on your token distribution; we ran a histogram and suggested bumping from 64 to 96 tokens for your top 20% long prompts.
[05:08] Sarah: ok great. what’s the plan for the 24h run?
[05:11] Liam: we will implement prompt canonicalization on the edge and accept a template_id header. then run a 24h live benchmark on your production-like traffic (we will mask PII). we'll capture KV/prefix hit rates, per-model latency, token cost, and eviction counts.
[05:24] Tom: timeline?
[05:25] Liam: aim to start on Thursday night after you push the small client header change. run 24h, then share results within 24 hours of completion.
[05:33] Maya: we’ll also provide the raw telemetry link and a derive spreadsheet (benchmarks.xlsx).
[05:38] Sarah: ok we’ll add a template_id header. one practical question: how do we map template ids to prompt templates in our repo?
[05:44] Liam: simplest is a short mapping file versioned in your repo (template_id -> template string). we can also support hashing the template server-side if you don’t want to transmit full template text. but recommending explicit template_id so you can roll versions.
[05:56] Priya: for rollout safety, any chance this will change model outputs or degrade quality? we can run A/B tests?
[06:02] Liam: canonicalization affects only cache keys and should not change model outputs. but to be safe, we recommend an A/B: route 10% of traffic without canonicalization, compare quality regressions on a small eval prompt set. Redwood Console will track quality regressions tied to prompt sets.
[06:18] Maya: perfect. quick housekeeping: i’ll send the security FAQ and the bench file. next sync we’ll review 24h run and discuss eviction tuning.
[06:26] Tom: sounds good. any blockers?
[06:28] Sarah: none from our side, just need the mapping change deployed.
[06:31] Maya: ok we’ll follow up. thanks everyone.
[06:34] (end)
